annotations.title: The Projection Map: m Candidates to 2
annotations.content: The key insight is that 'leads all combined' only cares about candidate 0 vs everyone else. The projection maps each vote to +1 (candidate 0) or -1 (any other), collapsing m candidates to a binary sequence. This is exact, not approximate.

annotations.title: Prefix Sum Preservation
annotations.content: The projection preserves prefix sums: the running tally of candidate 0's lead over all opponents combined is the same whether computed from the m-candidate sequence or the projected 2-candidate sequence. This means 'leads throughout' in the multi-candidate sense iff 'leads throughout' in the binary sense.

annotations.title: Fiber Uniformity: The Heart of the Proof
annotations.content: Each binary pattern (specifying which positions have candidate-0 votes) has exactly b!/(a₁!·...·aₘ₋₁!) multi-candidate refinements, where aᵢ are the vote counts for non-zero candidates. Since this count depends only on the vote totals (not the pattern), the conditional probability of 'leading throughout' equals the unconditional probability in the 2-candidate case.

annotations.title: Connecting to Mathlib's Classical Ballot Theorem
annotations.content: The projected sequences are shown to be elements of Mathlib's countedSequence type from Archive.Wiedijk100Theorems.BallotProblem. This allows direct application of the classical ballot theorem P = (a-b)/(a+b) to the projected sequences.

annotations.title: The Full Ordering Problem
annotations.content: A harder open question: what is the probability that candidate 0 leads each individual opponent (not just all combined) throughout? This cannot be reduced to a 2-candidate problem because leading opponents individually is a stronger condition than leading their combination. Different projection targets may interfere.
